This step is unnecessary for distilled, one-step models, where perturbations apply directly to the input noise. 4 Experimental Setup 4.1 Task Domain We assess the efficacy of our method in the domain of text-to-image generation. We conduct our primary evaluation on SDXL-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) , selected for its efficiency. To ensure our findings hold across diverse semantic contexts, we utilise the Parti Prompts benchmark ( Yu et al., 2022 ) . For SDXL-Turbo, we sample three prompts from each of the provided categories (e.g., abstract, complex), resulting in a diverse set of 36 evaluation tasks. To demonstrate the generality of our framework, we conduct additional experiments using the FLUX.1 [dev] model ( Labs, 2024 ) which utilises a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) architecture and relies on a multi-step generation process (typically 30-50 steps), in contrast to the U-Net-based, single-step generation of SDXL-Turbo. Due to the substantial computational cost associated with the Flux model, we restricted this evaluation to a subset of 12 12 prompts. Further implementation details are provided in Appendix Appendix C . Fitness Definition The fitness is the fidelity of the images to the prompt, quantified via the CLIP score ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , a standard metric for image-text alignment. Feature Definition We use DreamSim ( Fu et al., 2023 ) for our features. The model generates 768-dimensional embeddings trained to approximate human similarity judgements, thereby serving as a proxy for semantic distinctiveness. Genotype As noted in Section 3.2 , the spectral variation operator is general and can operate on any genotype. For each model, we define the genotype to encompass all available input components, splitting the batch size equally among them. We apply the same genotype definitions to all applicable baselines. An ablation study isolating each genotype component is provided in Section D.2 . 4.2 Baselines An overview of each baseline is provided below. A comprehensive related works and implementation details of baselines are provided in Appendices Appendix B and Section C.3 respectively. Framework Baselines We compare the QD-Diffusion framework design to the following baselines: • CVT-ME: A variant of MAP-Elites designed to scale to high-dimensional spaces by using Centroidal Voronoi Tessellations to discretise the feature space into a fixed number of cells ( Vassiliades et al., 2018 ) . • CMA-ES: A robust evolutionary optimisation strategy designed for high-dimensional spaces ( Hansen and Ostermeier, 1996 ) . Unlike QD algorithms, CMA-ES does not use a feature space and aims solely to maximise fitness. • CMA-MAE: A state-of-the-art Quality-Diversity algorithm that combines CMA-ES with the MAP-Elites archiving mechanism ( Fontaine and Nikolaidis, 2023 ) . While traditionally reliant on hand-defined feature spaces, we adapt this baseline to use a CVT-ME grid over DreamSim embeddings to ensure a fair comparison within our automated, high-dimensional feature setting. • Adam: Gradient-based optimisation of the latent variable over the fitness function ( Kingma, 2014 ) . • QDHF: Quality-Diversity via Human Feedback ( Ding et al., 2023 ) . This method uses CLIP embeddings as features and a learned projection layer to map high-dimensional embeddings to a low-dimensional latent space suitable for standard MAP-Elites. The learned layer is trained using a contrastive loss for similarity, with DreamSim serving as a proxy for human judgements. The CVT-ME, CMA-MAE and QDHF baselines are selected to determine whether our framework is the optimal QD algorithm for high-dimensional feature embeddings. Crucially, CVT-ME and QDHF employ our proposed spectral mutation operator, ensuring that comparisons isolate the efficacy of the archive mechanism rather than the variation strategy. CMA-ES and Adam represent pure fitness-maximising algorithms, while serving to test whether an explicit diversity mechanism is necessary or if powerful optimisers can implicitly discover diversity. Adam and QDHF are not evaluated on Flux due to computational constraints (see Appendix Section C.3 ). Variation Operator Baselines To isolate the efficacy of the h h -space Spectral Mutation operator from the framework, we benchmark it against the following variation operators: • Random seeds: A baseline wherein each iteration samples a batch of solutions via new random seeds, representing the standard usage pattern of diffusion models. • Diverse-Diffusion: A recent approach designed to enhance image variety by performing a search for latent vectors with maximum pairwise distance ( Zameshina et al., 2023 ) . • Particle Guidance: generates a batch of samples jointly rather than i.i.d., adding a guidance term that repels particles from one another to enforce within-batch diversity ( Corso et al., 2023 ) . • ImageBreeder: An evolutionary operator originally designed for image generation that performs latent-space crossover using a variety of strategies, including weighted blending and slicing along channels or spatial dimensions ( Sobania et al., 2025 ) . This is the only operator that is only applied to the latent noise vectors, as the operator was developed specifically for latent-space crossover. • Gaussian Noise: Adds isotropic perturbations to the genotype, defined as 𝐱 ′ = 𝐱 + σ ​ ϵ , \mathbf{x}^{\prime}=\mathbf{x}+\sigma\bm{\epsilon}, where ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) and σ \sigma is the mutation strength hyperparameter. • Isoline-DD: Generates offspring by perturbing a parent 𝐱 1 \mathbf{x}_{1} along the direction relative to a second parent 𝐱 2 \mathbf{x}_{2} , defined as 𝐱 ′ = σ 1 ​ 𝐱 1 + σ 2 ​ 𝒩 ​ ( 0 , 1 ) ​ ( 𝐱 1 − 𝐱 2 ) \mathbf{x}^{\prime}=\sigma_{1}\mathbf{x}_{1}+\sigma_{2}\mathcal{N}(0,1)(\mathbf{x}_{1}-\mathbf{x}_{2}) where σ 1 \sigma_{1} and σ 2 \sigma_{2} are hyperparameters ( Vassiliades and Mouret, 2018 ) . • Intermediate-Layer Gaussian noise: Instead of performing SVD-based updates at the intermediate timestep, we apply Gaussian noise to the intermediate vector 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} and then invert the process using the deterministic scheduler. The Random Seeds baseline provides a naive reference point; by contrast, Diverse Diffusion and Particle Guidance are sampling-based methods explicitly designed to promote diversity, and serve as non-evolutionary benchmarks. Since Particle Guidance operate through classifier-free guidance, it is inapplicable to one-step models and are therefore only evaluated on Flux. ImageBreeder allows for comparison to diffusion-specific evolutionary operators, while Gaussian Noise and IsoLine represent standard evolutionary baselines. The Intermediate-Layer Gaussian baseline is critical for demonstrating that meaningful diversity results from spectral mutation specifically, rather than performing mutation at intermediate layers. Hyperparameters For SDXL-Turbo, a computational budget of 2000 evaluations is allocated to all algorithms; for QD algorithms, this is processed as batches of 16 over 125 iterations. Flux experiments used a reduced computational budget of 400 total evaluations, processed as 100 100 iterations with a batch size of 4 4 . Statistical significance is determined using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Holm-Bonferroni correction ( Wilcoxon, 1992 ; Holm, 1979 ) . Further hyperparameter details and an ablation study on these choices are provided in Appendices Section C.1 and Appendix D respectively. 4.3 Evaluation Metrics Our primary metric is the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) which is a widely-used metric that measures both the quality and diversity of solutions, compared to a set of real images ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) . This metric is not reported for algorithms that fail to discover a significant number of solutions. We provide further implementation details in Appendix Section C.6 . Since the FID metric aggregates the Fitness and Diversity of solutions into one, we provide further insight via the following metrics: • Total Fitness: The total fitness scores of all solutions in the final collection, reflecting both the quality of individual solutions and the algorithm’s ability to populate the archive with solutions exceeding the fitness threshold. • Diversity (Mean Pairwise Distance): The average Euclidean distance between all pairs of embeddings in the final collection, quantifying the semantic spread of the discovered portfolio. • Number of Solutions: The total count of distinct solutions maintained in the final archive. 5 Results 5.1 Framework Results We first evaluate our framework using the FID score, as reported in Table 2 . By exploiting the spectral properties of the generative prior through our novel h h -space Spectral Mutation operator, our method effectively navigates high-dimensional latent manifolds to uncover diverse, high-fidelity portfolios of solutions. Our empirical validation was conducted on the domain of text-to-image generation, where our method consistently outperforms 12 12 baselines across two architectures in terms of FID score, demonstrating a superior balance of image quality and diversity. While the framework was designed to be domain-agnostic, this cross-domain generalisability remains to be validated empirically.
